clinical_category: Limb loss - body image, social withdrawal, and psychosocial adjustment
blueprint_topic: Therapeutic communication, coping assessment, and individualized psychosocial support after major body change
stem: Several weeks after a lower-limb amputation, a client says, "I avoid seeing friends because I do not want anyone to see me like this. I do not feel like myself anymore." Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Explore the client's feelings and goals without assuming everyone responds the same way, assess mood, coping and social withdrawal, and offer individualized resources such as a psychologist, social worker, or peer counselor if the client wants or needs additional support.
options.B: Tell the client that appearance should not matter and redirect the conversation to prosthetic training so negative feelings are not reinforced.
options.C: Require attendance at a peer-support group because every person with an amputation needs the same psychosocial intervention to adjust successfully.
options.D: Avoid discussing body image or social withdrawal because psychological adjustment is separate from rehabilitation and does not affect quality of life or participation.

rationale: A is correct. Current VA/DoD amputation-rehabilitation guidance treats psychosocial limitations and quality of life as integral parts of rehabilitation, not separate from physical recovery. VA patient guidance recognizes that limb loss can produce varied emotional responses and recommends listening to the individual's needs; a psychologist, social worker, or peer counselor can provide additional support when appropriate. B minimizes the client's expressed concern and shuts down therapeutic communication. C is overly prescriptive because support needs and preferences vary; peer support is a resource, not a mandatory intervention for every client. D incorrectly separates psychosocial recovery from rehabilitation. The final item therefore tests individualized assessment and support rather than assuming a uniform body-image response after amputation.
educational_objective: Use therapeutic communication after limb loss to assess individualized body-image concerns, mood, coping and social participation and connect the client with preferred psychosocial resources without minimizing or universalizing the adjustment process.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense; Veterans Health Administration
source_document_title: Rehabilitation of Lower Limb Amputation (2025); What to Expect: The Months After Amputation Surgery; Understanding Leg Amputation: Surgery for a Medical Condition
source_version_date: VA/DoD CPG 2025, VA page last updated 2026-07-09; Veterans Health Library page annual review 2026-04-01; current resources accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: VA/DoD 'Rehabilitation of Lower Limb Amputation (2025)' → rehabilitation framework addresses physical, functional and psychosocial outcomes and quality of life throughout post-amputation care. Veterans Health Library 'What to Expect: The Months After Amputation Surgery' → When to contact your amputation team: psychologist or peer counselor if more emotional support is needed; social worker for support resources. Veterans Health Library 'Understanding Leg Amputation' → Living with limb loss: emotional responses vary; consider psychologist or peer support; family/friends should listen and let the person identify what support is needed.
source_claim_supported: Current VA/DoD and VA patient resources directly support individualized psychosocial assessment after limb loss and optional referral to psychology, social work or peer support according to the client's needs and preferences.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: use therapeutic communication; assess coping, self-concept, mood and psychosocial responses to health alterations; provide support and coordinate referrals/resources when indicated.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic body-image-support list into an applied therapeutic-response scenario. The final version avoids assuming that all clients experience identical body-image concerns or mandating peer support, and instead tests individualized assessment, validation and resource coordination within the broader rehabilitation process.
audit_findings: The source's psychosocial concept was valid but presented as a generic support list and risked implying a uniform body-image response after amputation.
Fresh VA/DoD review directly supports psychosocial outcomes and quality of life as integral components of amputation rehabilitation.
Current VA patient guidance supports psychologist, social worker and peer-counselor resources when needed while emphasizing individualized emotional responses and support preferences.
Distractors test minimization, mandatory one-size-fits-all peer support and false separation of psychosocial care from rehabilitation; none is defensible.
